definition: A relationship in which one person (the agent) is authorized to act on behalf of another (the principal) in dealings with third parties.
The person who hires an agent and is owed fiduciary duties. Also called the client.
A party to a transaction who is not represented by the agent. Owed honesty and fair dealing, not fiduciary duties.
An agent authorized to do anything the principal could lawfully do, such as under a broad power of attorney.
An agent authorized to handle a range of matters in a particular business, like a property manager, or a salesperson for their broker.
An agent authorized to do one specific task, like a listing broker finding a buyer. Most real estate brokers are special agents of their clients.
An agent of an agent: for example, a cooperating broker who works for the listing broker on behalf of the seller.
One agent or brokerage representing both buyer and seller in the same transaction. Requires informed written consent where allowed.
A broker assigns different licensees in the same firm to represent the buyer and the seller separately. Nevada uses the term assigned agency.
A licensee who helps parties complete a deal without representing either one. Also called a facilitator; the term and its rules vary by state.
Representing only one party in a transaction.
An agency created by a stated agreement, oral or written, such as a listing or buyer agreement.
An agency created by the conduct of the agent and principal, without a stated agreement.
Creating agency after the fact, when a principal approves an act the agent did without authority.
Agency the law recognizes because the principal led a third party to reasonably believe someone was their agent.
An agency in which the agent has an ownership interest in the property. The principal cannot revoke it.
An agent ending the agency by giving it up. The agent may be liable for damages if it breaches the contract.
A principal ending the agency by withdrawing the agent's authority. The principal may owe damages if it breaches the contract.
A person in a position of trust who must act in the best interest of another. An agent is a fiduciary to the principal.
A memory aid for the fiduciary duties: Obedience, Loyalty, Disclosure, Confidentiality, Accounting, Reasonable care.
The duty to follow the principal's lawful instructions.
The duty to put the principal's interests above everyone else's, including the agent's own.
The duty to tell the principal every material fact the agent learns that could affect the principal's decisions.
The duty to keep the principal's private information private. It continues after the agency ends.
The duty to safeguard and account for all money and property received for the principal.
The duty to use the skill and care a competent licensee would use.
A written document giving someone (an attorney-in-fact) authority to act for another. Real estate uses must usually be recorded to convey property.
A false statement or concealment of a material fact. It may be intentional (fraud) or negligent.
An intentional misrepresentation of a material fact that someone relies on and is harmed by.
A false statement made without reasonable care to find out the truth, even without intent to deceive.
Exaggerated opinions, like "best view in town," that a reasonable person wouldn't take as fact. Not misrepresentation, but crossing into false facts is.
A fact that would affect a reasonable person's decision to buy, sell, or set a price.
A hidden defect not discoverable by ordinary inspection, such as a cracked slab under flooring.
"Let the buyer beware." The old rule that buyers take property as is. Modern disclosure laws limit it heavily.
Telling the parties in writing whom the licensee represents, at the time and in the form state law requires.
A situation where the licensee's own interests, or another client's, could pull against the client's interests.
An agent acting for their own benefit in a client's transaction, such as secretly buying the listing. Prohibited without full disclosure and consent.
Money or benefit an agent receives in a transaction without the principal's knowledge. A breach of loyalty.
Representing both parties without telling them and getting consent. A serious violation that can cost the agent the commission and the license.
A payment to another licensee for referring a client. Must be disclosed and paid through the broker as state law requires.
